https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/01/new-.text: Menü Kereső Két embert is megkéselt egy nő a New York-i Times Square-en, mielőtt lelőtték a rendőrök Külföld Egy rendőr őrködik a New York-i Times Square azon részén, ahol az eset történt – Fotó: Brendan McDermid / TPX Images of the Day / Reuters Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Egy 32 éves nőt halálra késeltek, egy férfi pedig megsérült kedden New Yorkban, miután valaki rájuk támadt a város kvázi főterén, a Times Square-en – írja a BBC . A támadó egy nő volt, aki két késsel hadonászott és támadott a járókelőkre, majd a rendőrök lelőtték. Mindhárom sérültet még élve vitték kórházba, de a támadó és egyik áldozata a kórházban meghalt Zohran Mamdani polgármester szerint. A meghalt áldozatot később Erin Piacentiként, a Bank of America egyik alkalmazottjaként azonosították. A Reuters arról írt, Piacenti a bank egy részlegének az alelnöke volt, aki az üzleti kiválasztási és konfliktuskezelési osztályon dolgozott. A bank manhattani irodái egyébként kőhajításnyira vannak a Times Square-től. A másik megkéselt személy, egy 68 éves férfi állapota stabil. Jessica Tisch rendőrtiszt szerint a késeléseket nem provokálták ki az áldozatok, azok között mintegy 20 másodperc eltelt. Szerinte a rendőrséget helyi idő szerint délután 16:24-kor értesítették. A támadó először a metróból a feleségével feljövő férfire rontott rá, és a hasa jobb oldalán megszúrta. A késelő ezután továbbment a Hetedik sugárúton, majd itt szúrta meg a később meghalt áldozatot. Ekkor érkezett meg a rendőrség, és négy percen keresztül győzködte a nőt, hogy dobja el a kést. „Nem dobok el semmit, inkább megöllek titeket” – felelte a nő, majd többszöri fenyegetés után elindult a rendőrök felé. A sokkoló sem állította meg, ezért rálőttek. A támadót később a 49 éves Pamela Cisnerosként azonosították, akit ugyan sosem ítéltek el, de mentálisan instabil volt, már 2018-tól akadtak ügyei a rendőrséggel. Photograph: Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images View image in fullscreen A spokesperson from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration said the agency is investigating Roberts’ death. Photograph: Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images Missouri Missouri UPS worker two weeks from retirement fatally struck by company vehicle Paul Roberts, who was employed by UPS for 44 years, was working at a customer care center when he was struck Ramon Antonio Vargas Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A longtime United Parcel Service (UPS) employee less than two weeks away from retiring was struck and killed by one of the company’s vehicles while he was at work in St Louis, triggering a federal labor investigation along with an intense outpouring of grief from his family and colleagues. Paul Roberts, 63, was on duty at the UPS customer care center in Earth City, Missouri , on the night of 4 September when a company vehicle hit him, authorities said. Roberts, of nearby St Charles, Missouri , died at the scene. The vehicle’s driver cooperated with investigators who responded to reports of the fatal accident, local police said in a statement provided to the Guardian on Thursday. Missouri state legislative candidate accused of trying to plant cocaine on opponent Read more The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) is investigating Roberts’ death, a process that could take up to six months, an agency spokesperson said in a separate statement on Thursday. While neither Osha nor the police released more details, Roberts’ story quickly gained attention beyond St Louis because family members told local news media that he had planned to retire on 17 September after 44 years of working at UPS. Roberts had started with UPS sorting packages as a teenager, eventually working various jobs for the delivery company over the ensuing decades, the St Louis Post-Dispatch newspaper reported . He had most recently operated as a feeder truck driver and was looking forward to gardening while collecting his retirement benefits, having only married his wife, Barb, in March after 37 years together, according to the newspaper, which spoke to Roberts’ sister, Donna Schraer. “It’s just unbelievable – that close to finally [being] able to relax,” Schraer told the Post-Dispatch. The St Louis news station KSDK separately reported that it was contacted by UPS employees who were worried “about the dark conditions the night Roberts was killed, in addition to ongoing safety concerns”. Asked for comment about Roberts on Thursday, UPS spokesperson Jim Mayer said in a statement to the Guardian: “We focus on the safety of our people every day. We train our people to prevent accidents and injuries and teach them how to stay healthy and safe.” Mayer’s statement said UPS “invested more than 35[m] hours and over $2[bn] on safety training” since 2021. His statement also said: “We’re saddened by the tragic situation in Earth City. Our heartfelt thoughts are with the family, friends and coworkers of our team member.” Osha did not list any other fatalities at the site where Roberts was killed, according to agency information cited by the Post-Dispatch. But the newspaper also noted that two past workplace incidents reported there resulted in amputations, and others resulted in heat-related injuries, though none involved vehicles. The Teamsters Local 688 labor union to which Roberts belonged described his death as “a tragedy”. The union’s statement also said: “Our members’ safety is priority one when on the job.” Besides Roberts’ sister and wife, his survivors include his children and grandchildren, KSDK reported. They all would remember his legacy as a “hard-working family man”, she told the channel. “It’s sad he’s not going to be able to celebrate” his retirement with his loved ones, Schraer also told KSDK. “I hate just being shocked that this is all going on right now.” Explore more on these topics Missouri Couriers/delivery industry news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/unions-m.text: BRIGHTON, England — Britain’s trade unions are preparing to back a suite of changes to political finance rules after two cryptocurrency tycoons donated a record £72 million to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Unions had been lobbying the governing Labour Party — to which they gave around £5 million in 2025 — against introducing an annual cap on U.K.-based individual donors, on the basis that it could curb their donations too. But in the wake of Reform’s unprecedented haul, unions are now planning to shift that position and back the idea of further reforms to both spending and donations, two senior union officials not authorized to speak publicly told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement Farage — who is already facing investigations into his right-wing populist party’s funding sources — announced over the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, had donated £36 million each. Each of those donations was record-breaking in British politics, which currently sets no upper limit on what U.K.-based individuals can hand to a party. Together, they have reignited a row about Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s position on funding. He has so far held off on imposing a cap on domestic donations to political parties. Nigel Farage addresses delegates during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Anthony Devlin/Getty Images Both officials quoted above said the Trades Union Congress — which is this week hosting its annual conference in Brighton — is expected to issue a joint statement setting out an updated position on political financing, which could be released as soon as Tuesday. But the talks are politically delicate and the unions have not yet reached agreement. One of the two senior officials said unions are likely to back a cap that applies to wealthy U.K.-based individuals and to trade unions, but — crucially — would be calculated in different ways for these two types of donor. That would mean that while wealthy individuals and unions would both be subject to donations caps, the rules would apply differently for each group. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told union members Monday: “We will defend our democracy and society from any foreign dictator or fascist oligarch who seeks to divide our country and buy our politics — but we will never undermine the rights of working people to organize collectively and democratically.” Advertisement Advertisement Separately, unions are also discussing whether to back a review of how political parties spend their money, both officials quoted above said. Party spending is currently regulated retrospectively for the year before an election, and limits tighten further in the final weeks. This would mirror a move from the Labour government, which tasked the Electoral Commission earlier this summer with reviewing spending limits on political campaigning and reporting back by July 2027. Angela Rayner speaks at the Trades Union Congress in Brighton on Sept. 14, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images The first official quoted above said: “If that money’s already landed [with Reform] and it’s going to stay there, it’s about how much you can spend on, for example, social media advertising.” Change of topic The issue has dominated the start of the TUC’s annual gathering of 47 trade unions, 11 of which have formal financial ties to Labour. The TUC already opposes donations by overseas residents and those which are given in the form of cryptocurrency. It has led to a fierce tussle between unions on the campaigning left, which want to take firmer action against mega-donations, and those closest to Labour that fear their own funding of the party will be undercut. Some union officials also fear that supporting one set of rules for trade unions and a different set for wealthy individuals will be seized upon by opponents on the right. The first union official quoted above insisted they “wouldn’t describe it as a carve-out,” given rules would apply to both groups. Advertisement Advertisement But Reform’s Deputy Leader Richard Tice has already accused Labour of “hyperventilating hypocrisy” for looking at changing the rules. Union leaders spent Monday trying to emphasize the difference in the way unions and individuals fund political parties. Many union donations to Labour are paid in the form of “affiliation fees” from hundreds of thousands of individual members. TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak told union members on Monday: “Let no one tell you there is any similarity between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union, and a party bought and paid for by billionaires.” Nowak speaks at the Trades Union Congress in Brighton on Sept. 14, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images He later told ITV News: “You’ve got to design the rules in the right way. What we don’t want to do is exclude the voices of workers.” The debate was still ongoing behind closed doors at the TUC on Monday. Andrea Egan, the left-wing head of public services union UNISON, told BBC News “there shouldn’t be a cap on trade union donations” but added the details should be looked at. Back in Westminster, Labour MPs who have been pushing for a domestic cap were encouraged by the thawing of union opposition — but they are turning to the House of Lords to keep up the pressure on the government. Advertisement Advertisement Former justice minister, and Labour peer Michael Wills, is preparing to put forward his own amendment supporting their cause when the Bill reaches its next stage. He will take the baton from Stella Creasy, the MP whose amendment to introduce a £100,000 cap was not debated in the Commons after the government agreed to initiate a taskforce on the subject earlier this month. She said the weekend’s donations must represent a “wake-up call.” Cap that Questions remain over whether Reform will be able to accept the £72 million donations because both Delo and Harborne could be caught by the separate £100,000 cap on overseas donations that will be introduced under existing legislation. Richard Tice delivers a speech at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham on Sept. 4, 2026. | Anthony Devlin/Getty Images Delo has been living in Hong Kong, and Harborne in Thailand. Both planned to change their voter registration so they can still donate. But the law change will be backdated to March 25 this year — making that a crucial cut-off to avoid being hit by the cap. Farage hinted that the record-breaking donations might not survive the existing government proposals. In an interview, he told the BBC they are “100% compliant with the law today” — but declined to say, crucially, whether the donors were resident by the March 25 cutoff date. He criticized how the legislation will apply retrospectively. Advertisement Advertisement Tice, Farage’s deputy, told GB News the legislation amounted to an attempt to “rig the system” against Reform. The attempt to curtail the donations comes as Reform faces controversy about money linked to the party on multiple fronts. Two of Farage’s closest advisers stepped down earlier this month after being caught in an undercover sting concerning donations. Farage remains under separate investigation by parliamentary authorities over his alleged failure to declare a £5 million “gift” from Harborne before the 2024 general election — plus support from a convicted fraudster.

Viewpoints Opinion China Exported Its Battery Factories to Europe—and Its Contempt for Environmental Rules Chinese battery factories in Hungary have been hit by a series of environmental and regulatory problems. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Protesters hold Hungarian flags and a poster reading 'Clean water and clean air' during a demonstration against the plans of Chinese battery giant CATL to build Europe's largest gigafactory, in Debrecen, Hungary, on Feb. 4, 2023. Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images Xiao Yi 10/4/2026 | Updated: 10/7/2026 0:00 X 1 Commentary For nearly a decade, Hungary served as the red carpet for China’s global electric-vehicle ambitions. Courted by Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s Beijing-friendly “Eastern Opening” policy, Chinese industrial giants were showered with billions of euros in state subsidies, prime real estate, and expedited regulatory shortcuts designed to bypass environmental scrutiny. The crown jewels of this arrangement—CATL’s mega battery cell plant and Semcorp’s separator film facility—chose Hungary’s second city of Debrecen as their launchpad to supply automotive powerhouses such as BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen. Today, that gold rush is unraveling into a catastrophic compliance and environmental crisis. Facing revelations of toxic industrial solvent spills, groundwater heavy-metal contamination thousands of times above legal limits, and a seismic shift in Hungarian politics, Chinese battery manufacturers are discovering that the shortcuts that fueled their domestic rise do not work in Europe. CATL’s ‘Green Dye’ Defense Crumbles In August 2022, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL), the world’s largest battery manufacturer, pledged 7.34 billion euros ($8.33 billion) to build a 100-gigawatt-hour plant in Debrecen, the largest foreign direct investment in Hungarian history. The project was celebrated as a milestone that would establish Hungary as Europe’s second-largest EV battery manufacturer. Related Stories 🎧 The Hidden Risks of Buying a Repurposed EV Battery EV Adoption Risks a China-Controlled Battery Crisis In May, the project’s honeymoon abruptly ended when a foul-smelling, neon-green liquid bubbled out of stormwater drains adjacent to the plant and spilled onto surrounding public streets. CATL dismissed the incident as a benign plumbing overflow, claiming that the water came from standard pressure-testing equipment and that food-grade green dye had merely been added to trace pipeline leaks. Independent laboratory testing commissioned by local civil groups immediately punctured the company’s narrative. The samples contained manganese levels three times higher than the national drinking water safety threshold, alongside elevated traces of lithium, nickel, and cobalt. Most alarming was the detection of N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP)—an industrial solvent integral to electrode coating that does not occur in nature. NMP is classified under European Union regulations as a toxic substance that damages fertility and unborn children. Follow-up government inspections exposed systemic violations: The plant had illegally tapped internal wastewater lines directly into the municipal drainage network, allowing hazardous industrial effluent to bypass standard detoxification facilities. Hungarian media outlet 24.hu reported on May 28, citing lawmaker Zsolt Tárkányi, that a government office had withdrawn a previously issued water-authority approval for CATL’s Debrecen plant and imposed a fine of 1 million forints (about $3,100). On June 5, authorities said the water authority had revoked the plant’s permit to pretreat industrial wastewater and had ordered CATL to clean the municipal wastewater and stormwater drainage networks. On Aug. 24, the Hungarian Ministry of Transport and Investment announced that CATL had been fined 10 million forints (about $31,000) for breaching its integrated environmental permit. Inspectors had found deficiencies in waste labeling, storage, and record-keeping at the plant, among other violations. Concurrently, authorities abolished blanket environmental exemptions for major strategic investments, barring non-compliant developers from obtaining new building permits for six months. Semcorp Faces Criminal Charges Over Toxic Plume While CATL grapples with permit revocations, Yunnan Energy New Material’s separator subsidiary, Semcorp, faces an existential legal reckoning just miles away. Occupying 47 acres in Debrecen’s southern industrial park, Semcorp’s 183 million euros ($212 million) facility was designed to produce 400 million square meters of wet-process battery separator films annually. In February, a ruptured pipeline discharged a steaming, pungent liquid directly into the surrounding soil. Emulating CATL’s public relations playbook, Semcorp initially downplayed the event as an innocuous release of “condensed water with no harmful components.” The official environmental report, however, painted a horrifying picture. Groundwater near the facility showed aluminum concentrations of 2.676 million micrograms per liter—a staggering 13,000 times above statutory limits—alongside dangerous levels of arsenic, lead, cadmium, and cobalt. The contamination was traced to the plant’s alumina coating workshops, representing a direct, acute threat to local aquifers and drinking water reserves. By July, regional environmental and fire safety agencies had issued sweeping shutdown orders, suspending all factory operations over structural hazards and malfunctioning emergency systems. Debrecen Mayor László Papp publicly demanded that Semcorp leave Debrecen, while the municipal government referred the company to state prosecutors for criminal liability. When Political Favors Expire For years, Hungary stood as the crown jewel of Europe for Chinese green-energy investment. The partnership was driven by mutual convenience: Budapest sought to modernize its industrial base by welcoming foreign giants such as CATL and BYD, while Chinese firms capitalized on Hungary’s strategic proximity to German and Central European automakers to secure a vital bridgehead into the EU’s massive single market. The arrangement was a straightforward exchange: Chinese battery makers invested in Hungarian factories and gained a foothold in the European market, while Hungary gained manufacturing capacity and jobs. Hungary offered prime land, substantial tax credits, direct cash subsidies, and expedited approvals. In return, Chinese conglomerates delivered billions in capital expenditure, industrial output, and export revenues. For Beijing’s corporate champions, Hungary was an ideal launchpad for replicating their domestic supply chains on European soil. Underpinning this expansion, however, was a reliance on an unwritten formula: Chinese capital and industrial capacity traded for political patronage, lax oversight, and administrative shortcuts. In essence, it was an attempt to export the domestic Chinese playbook—where local party officials routinely subordinate environmental protections to guarantee gross domestic product growth and employment quotas. That era ended decisively in April, when the center-right Tisza Party ousted Orbán’s long-ruling Fidesz government. The incoming administration took office on an explicit mandate to protect local natural resources and end corporate impunity, declaring “zero tolerance” for industrial battery pollution. Budapest is now preparing to establish a dedicated federal enforcement agency for heavy industrial polluters and is drafting legislation to replace fixed administrative fines with penalties calculated as a percentage of a company’s global annual turnover—a move that could expose non-compliant Chinese multinationals to hundreds of millions of euros in liability. Compounding this local reckoning is a tightening European regulatory net. The EU Batteries Regulation is adding new requirements for battery makers, including lifecycle carbon-footprint declarations for EV batteries and certain rechargeable industrial batteries. The effective dates for these declarations depend on further EU implementing rules. Starting on Feb. 18, 2027, all EV and industrial batteries with a capacity above 2 kilowatt-hours placed on the EU market will also require digital battery passports. The message for China’s outbound industrial champions is unambiguous: Environmental compliance cannot be treated as a post-construction afterthought. In mature democracies, independent journalism, empowered local residents, and independent courts cannot be swept aside by backroom understandings with friendly politicians. For Chinese executives who assumed European operations could be run like domestic industrial parks, Debrecen offers a sobering lesson: Without genuine respect for the rule of law, billions in foreign capital can turn into stranded assets overnight.
